title: The Brahmin and the Three Rogues
text:
A brahmin went to a nearby village to get an animal for a sacrifice. He came back with a fat goat, slung it over his shoulders and set off home through the forest.

Three rogues saw him and wanted the goat. They agreed on a plan and placed themselves at different points along his path.

The first stepped out in front of him and said, in a shocked voice, that he was amazed to see a holy man carrying a dog on his shoulders. Dogs were unclean; how could a brahmin touch one? The brahmin told him angrily that he was blind; it was a goat for a sacrifice. He walked on.

Further on, the second rogue stopped him and asked, just as shocked, why a brahmin was carrying a dead calf on his shoulders. The brahmin began to wonder. He put the goat down, looked at it carefully, picked it up again and went on, now uneasy.

Then the third rogue met him and asked, with disgust, why a holy man was carrying a donkey, an animal no brahmin should touch. Now the brahmin was sure that he was mistaken, or that some demon had bewitched him. Three men could not all be wrong. He threw the goat down, hurried off to bathe and purify himself, and the rogues took the goat home and ate it.
lesson: Trust your own evidence. When several people repeat the same claim, check whether they are independent witnesses or one interest speaking with several voices.
people: A brahmin, three rogues, a goat
caveat: In the Panchatantra the rogues call the goat a dog, a dead calf and a donkey; in the Hitopadesha version all three call it a dog.
